chapter_sections.label: DEFINITION:
chapter_sections.text:
A PURE SUBSTANCE consists of a single type of particle. All constituent particles
are the same in their chemical nature. A MIXTURE contains more than one pure
substance mixed in any proportion.

chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Matter is classified as pure substances and mixtures.
Pure substances have the same characteristic properties regardless of source.
A mixture shows properties of its constituent substances.
Pure substances are further classified as elements and compounds.
Mixtures are classified as homogeneous and heterogeneous.

chapter_sections.label: LIST OF TOPICS:
items: 2.4 What are the Types of Pure Substances?

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
A MIXTURE is constituted by more than one kind of pure form of matter. The
components of a mixture retain their individual properties and can be separated
by physical methods.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: A mixture has a variable composition -- different proportions can be mixed.
Properties of a mixture are the same as those of its constituting substances.
Most matter around us exists as mixtures -- sea water, minerals, soil, etc.
Mixtures can be separated into pure substances using appropriate methods.
A mixture contains more than one pure substance.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 2.1:
sections.aim: To distinguish homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures.
sections.materials:
Beakers, water, copper sulphate powder, potassium permanganate,
common salt, glass rod.
procedure: - Group A: 50 mL water + 1 spatula copper sulphate. Stir.
- Group B: 50 mL water + 2 spatulas copper sulphate. Stir.
- Groups C and D: Mix different amounts of copper sulphate and potassium
permanganate or common salt in water.
- Report observations on uniformity in colour and texture.
sections.observation:
- Groups A and B: Uniform colour throughout (homogeneous). Colour intensity
differs showing variable composition.
- Groups C and D: Physically distinct parts with non-uniform composition
(heterogeneous).
sections.conclusion:
Homogeneous mixtures have uniform composition throughout;
heterogeneous mixtures have non-uniform composition with distinct parts.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 2.2:
sections.aim: To observe solution, suspension, and colloidal solution.
sections.materials:
Beakers, water, copper sulphate, chalk powder, wheat flour, milk,
ink, glass rod, torch, filter paper, funnel.
procedure: - Group A: Copper sulphate in water.
- Group B: More copper sulphate in water.
- Group C: Chalk powder or wheat flour in water.
- Group D: Milk or ink in water.
- Add each sample to water, stir, check visibility of particles, pass torch
sections.observation:
- A and B: Particles not visible, stable, no light scattering, cannot filter.
- C: Particles visible, settles on standing, scatters light, can filter.
- D: Particles not visible to naked eye, stable, scatters light (Tyndall effect),
cannot filter.

items.question: What is a mixture? Give two examples.
items.answer:
A mixture is constituted by more than one kind of pure form of matter. Components
retain their individual properties and can be separated by physical methods.
Examples: Sea water (water + dissolved salts), soil (sand + clay + minerals).

items.question: Differentiate between homogeneous and heterogeneous mixtures.
items.answer:
HOMOGENEOUS MIXTURE: Uniform composition throughout. Components not seen
separately. Example: salt solution.
HETEROGENEOUS MIXTURE: Non-uniform composition with physically distinct parts.
Components visible separately. Example: mixture of iron filings and sulphur.

items.question: What are the key properties of a mixture? State three.
items.answer:
1. Variable composition: Components can be mixed in any proportion.
2. Retention of properties: Each component retains its individual chemical
properties.
3. Physical separation: Components can be separated by physical methods such as
filtration, evaporation, or use of magnet.

items.question: With the help of Activity 2.1, explain how you can show that a
items.answer:
Activity: Two beakers with 50 mL water each.
- Beaker A: 1 spatula of copper sulphate dissolved.
- Beaker B: 2 spatulas of copper sulphate dissolved.
Observation: Both beakers show uniform colour throughout (homogeneous), but
beaker B is darker than beaker A.
Conclusion: Both are homogeneous mixtures (uniform throughout), but their
compositions are different -- beaker A is dilute and beaker B is concentrated.
This proves that a homogeneous mixture can have variable composition.

items.question: Using Activity 2.2, explain how a solution, suspension, and
items.answer:
Solution (Groups A, B -- copper sulphate in water):
- Particles not visible, stable, does not settle, does not scatter light.

Suspension (Group C -- chalk in water):
- Particles visible to naked eye, unstable, settles on standing, can be
filtered, scatters light (path visible).

Colloidal Solution (Group D -- milk/ink in water):
- Particles not visible to naked eye, stable, does not settle, cannot be
filtered by ordinary filter paper, scatters light (Tyndall effect).

Key difference: particle size -- solution (<1 nm), colloid (1-1000 nm),
suspension (>1000 nm).

items.question: What is a mixture? Classify mixtures into types with definitions,
items.answer:
A mixture is constituted by more than one kind of pure form of matter. Components
retain their properties and can be separated by physical methods.

sections.label: CLASSIFICATION:
sections.text:
1. HOMOGENEOUS MIXTURE (Solution):
Definition: Uniform composition throughout.
Properties: Particles <1 nm, stable, no Tyndall effect, cannot be filtered.
Examples: Salt water, sugar water, air, alloys.

2. HETEROGENEOUS MIXTURE:
a) Suspension:
Definition: Coarse particles dispersed in a medium, visible to naked eye.
Properties: Settles on standing, scatters light, can be filtered.
Examples: Muddy water, chalk in water.

b) Colloid:
Definition: Particles too small to see but large enough to scatter light.
Properties: Stable, shows Tyndall effect, cannot filter by ordinary paper.
Examples: Milk, starch solution, fog, butter.

SEPARATION METHOD -- Filtration (for suspension):
- Pour muddy water through filter paper in a funnel.
- Mud particles are too large to pass through filter paper (residue).
- Clear water passes through as filtrate.
- Components are separated based on particle size difference.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Which of the following is a homogeneous mixture?
items.explanation: Salt solution has uniform composition throughout -- salt evenly distributed in water. Oil and water, sand and salt, and soil are heterogeneous.

items.question: Which property allows mixture components to be separated?
items.explanation: Components retain individual properties in a mixture, so physical methods exploit these differences. Options A and D describe pure substances.

items.question: A suspension differs from a solution because:
items.explanation: Suspension particles (>1000 nm) settle on standing -- it is unstable. Solutions are stable and do not settle. Suspensions can be filtered.

items.question: In Activity 2.2, which group obtained a colloidal solution?
items.explanation: Milk and ink form colloids -- particles 1-1000 nm, stable, Tyndall effect visible. Group C forms suspension. Groups A and B form true solutions.

items.question: A homogeneous mixture can have variable composition. This is demonstrated by:

options.B: different concentrations of copper sulphate both giving uniform solutions

items.explanation: Different amounts of copper sulphate dissolved in water give dilute and concentrated solutions -- both homogeneous but different composition.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of a mixture?
items.explanation: Fixed composition is a characteristic of pure substances especially compounds. Mixtures always have variable composition.

items.question: Iron filings and sulphur can be separated using a magnet. This is possible because:

options.B: components of a mixture retain their individual properties
options.C: iron and sulphur form a compound

items.explanation: In a mixture, components retain their properties. Iron retains its magnetic property and is attracted by magnet; sulphur is non-magnetic and stays behind.

items.question: Tyndall effect is shown by colloidal solutions but not by true solutions because:

options.B: colloid particles (1-1000 nm) are large enough to scatter light unlike

items.explanation: Colloidal particles (1-1000 nm) are in the size range to scatter visible light. Solution particles (<1 nm) are too small to scatter light -- beam passes through invisible.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
Depending upon the nature of the components forming a mixture, we can have
different types of mixtures -- HOMOGENEOUS and HETEROGENEOUS.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: HOMOGENEOUS MIXTURES:
Uniform composition throughout at particle level.
Components not visible separately.
Examples: salt dissolved in water, sugar in water, copper sulphate solution,
lemonade, soda water, air, alloys.
Can have variable composition (dilute vs concentrated).
HETEROGENEOUS MIXTURES:
Non-uniform composition with physically distinct parts.
Components visible separately.
Examples: iron filings and sulphur, salt and sand, oil and water, soil.
Further classified as suspension and colloidal solution.
COMPARISON TABLE:
Property         | Solution        | Colloid         | Suspension
Particle size    | Less than 1 nm  | 1 to 1000 nm    | More than 1000 nm
Visibility       | Not visible     | Not visible     | Visible (naked eye)
Tyndall effect   | No              | Yes             | Yes (but cloudy)
Stability        | Very stable     | Stable          | Unstable (settles)
Filtration       | Cannot filter   | Cannot filter   | Can filter
Example          | Salt water      | Milk, fog       | Muddy water

items.question: What is the Tyndall effect? Name two colloidal solutions that
items.answer:
The TYNDALL EFFECT is the scattering of a beam of visible light by colloidal
particles, making the path of light visible.
Examples showing Tyndall effect:
1. Milk (fat globules scattered in water -- emulsion colloid).
2. Starch solution (starch particles in water -- sol colloid).

items.question: Compare the properties of solution, suspension, and colloid based
items.answer:
Solution:
- Particle size: Less than 1 nm.
- Stability: Very stable, does not settle.
- Tyndall effect: No (particles too small to scatter light).

Colloid:
- Particle size: 1 to 1000 nm.
- Stability: Stable, does not settle.
- Tyndall effect: Yes (particles large enough to scatter light).

Suspension:
- Particle size: More than 1000 nm.
- Stability: Unstable, settles on standing.
- Tyndall effect: Yes (but also appears cloudy/turbid).

items.question: From the table of common examples of colloids, classify the
items.answer:
1. Fog: Aerosol type colloid.
Dispersed phase: Liquid (water droplets).
Dispersion medium: Gas (air).

2. Milk: Emulsion type colloid.
Dispersed phase: Liquid (fat).
Dispersion medium: Liquid (water).

3. Butter: Gel type colloid.
Dispersed phase: Liquid (fat).
Dispersion medium: Solid (protein matrix).

4. Smoke: Aerosol type colloid.
Dispersed phase: Solid (carbon particles).
Dispersion medium: Gas (air).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Which of the following is a colloidal solution?
items.explanation: Milk is a colloid (emulsion -- fat dispersed in water, particle size 1-1000 nm). Salt water and sugar water are solutions. Muddy water is a suspension.

items.question: Fog is an example of which type of colloid?
items.explanation: Fog = liquid (water droplets) dispersed in gas (air) = Aerosol type. Emulsion = liquid in liquid, Sol = solid in liquid, Gel = liquid in solid.

items.question: Which separation method is used for colloidal solutions?
items.explanation: Colloidal particles pass through ordinary filter paper so filtration fails. Centrifugation applies strong centrifugal force to separate colloidal particles. Evaporation and decantation are not suitable.

items.question: Butter is classified as which type of colloid?
items.explanation: Butter has liquid fat (dispersed phase) in solid protein-water matrix (dispersion medium) = Gel type colloid. Emulsion is liquid in liquid (like milk).

items.question: Sunlight passing through forest canopy shows a visible beam of light. This phenomenon is:

options.A: reflection of light from tree leaves
options.B: Tyndall effect -- mist droplets (colloid) scatter sunlight

items.explanation: Mist in forest contains water droplets of colloidal size (1-1000 nm). These scatter sunlight making the beam visible -- classic Tyndall effect. This is not reflection, refraction, or diffraction.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
A SOLUTION is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances. The major
component is called the SOLVENT and the minor component (dissolved substance)
is called the SOLUTE.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Solution has homogeneity at the particle level.
Particles smaller than 1 nm (10^-9 m) -- invisible to naked eye.
Solute particles do not scatter a beam of light -- path not visible.
Solute particles cannot be separated by filtration.
Solute particles do not settle down -- a solution is stable.
TYPES OF SOLUTIONS:
Solid in liquid: salt water, sugar water.
Liquid in liquid: lemonade, alcohol in water.
Gas in liquid: soda water (CO2 in water), aerated drinks.
Solid in solid: alloys (brass = zinc + copper, 30% Zn + 70% Cu).
Gas in gas: air.
DO YOU KNOW?
ALLOYS are mixtures of two or more metals or a metal and a non-metal. They cannot
be separated into components by physical methods. But an alloy is considered a
mixture because it shows properties of its constituents and can have variable
composition. Example: Brass is a mixture of approximately 30% zinc and 70% copper.

items.question: What is a solution? Name its two components.
items.answer:
A SOLUTION is a homogeneous mixture of two or more substances.
Two components:
1. SOLVENT: Component that dissolves the other; usually in larger quantity.
Example: water in salt water.
2. SOLUTE: Component dissolved in solvent; usually in smaller quantity.
Example: salt in salt water.

items.question: Define Tyndall effect. Give two everyday examples.
items.answer:
The TYNDALL EFFECT is the scattering of a beam of visible light by colloidal
particles, making the path of light visible.
Examples:
1. Sunlight passing through canopy of a dense forest (mist = water droplets in air).
2. A fine beam of light entering a room through a small hole (dust and smoke in air
scatter light).

items.question: What is a saturated solution? Describe with Activity 2.3 how
items.answer:
SATURATED SOLUTION: A solution in which no more solute can be dissolved at a
given temperature. The amount of solute present is called its SOLUBILITY.

sections.label: Activity 2.3:
sections.observation:
More solute dissolves on heating. Different substances dissolve in
different amounts at the same temperature.
sections.conclusion:
Solubility increases with temperature. Different substances have
different solubilities at the same temperature.

Q4 [4 Marks]: How is a suspension different from a colloidal solution? Give
properties and examples of each.
A4:
SUSPENSION:
- Heterogeneous mixture; particle size >1000 nm.
- Particles visible to naked eye.
- Unstable -- settles on standing.
- Can be separated by filtration.
- Scatters light (path visible, cloudy appearance).
Examples: muddy water, chalk in water.

COLLOIDAL SOLUTION:
- Heterogeneous (appears homogeneous); particle size 1-1000 nm.
- Particles not visible to naked eye.
- Stable -- does not settle.
- Cannot be separated by ordinary filtration; needs centrifugation.
- Shows Tyndall effect (clear scattering of beam).
Examples: milk, starch solution, fog.

Q5 [4 Marks]: Calculate the mass by mass percentage concentration of a solution
containing 40 g of common salt dissolved in 320 g of water.
A5:
Given:
Mass of solute (salt) = 40 g
Mass of solvent (water) = 320 g

Mass of solution = Mass of solute + Mass of solvent
= 40 + 320 = 360 g

Mass by mass percentage = (Mass of solute / Mass of solution) x 100
= (40 / 360) x 100
= 11.1%

Therefore, concentration of salt solution = 11.1% (mass by mass).
[This is Example 2.1 from textbook]

Q6 [6 Marks]: Explain in detail the three types of mixtures -- solution,
colloid, and suspension -- with their properties, examples, and methods of
separation.
A6:
Based on particle size, mixtures are classified as:

1. SOLUTION:
Particle size: Less than 1 nm.
Properties:
- Homogeneous; uniform composition.
- Particles not visible, stable, does not settle.
- Does not show Tyndall effect.
- Cannot be separated by filtration.
Separation: Evaporation (solid in liquid); distillation (liquid mixture).
Examples: Salt water, sugar water, air, brass (solid solution).

2. COLLOID:
Particle size: 1 nm to 1000 nm.
Properties:
- Appears homogeneous but actually heterogeneous.
- Particles not visible to naked eye.
- Stable, does not settle.
- Shows Tyndall effect.
- Cannot be filtered; separated by centrifugation.
Examples: Milk, fog, butter, starch solution, blood.

3. SUSPENSION:
Particle size: More than 1000 nm.
Properties:
- Heterogeneous; non-uniform.
- Particles visible to naked eye.
- Unstable -- settles on standing.
- Can be filtered.
Examples: Muddy water, chalk in water, wheat flour in water.

Importance: Understanding mixture type helps choose correct separation method
in industry (making medicines, water purification), food processing, and daily life.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: In a sugar solution, which component is the solute?
items.explanation: Solute is the component dissolved in solvent (present in smaller quantity). Sugar is dissolved in water, so sugar = solute, water = solvent.

items.question: Which of the following is NOT a property of a true solution?
items.explanation: Settling on standing is a property of suspension, not solution. Solution particles (<1 nm) are too small to settle -- solution is very stable.

items.question: A solution contains 20 g salt in 180 g water. Mass percentage is:
items.explanation: Mass of solution = 20 + 180 = 200 g. Percentage = (20/200) x 100 = 10%.

items.question: Alloys are considered mixtures because:

options.B: they show properties of constituents and have variable composition
options.D: they are formed by chemical reaction

items.explanation: Alloys show properties of constituent metals and can have variable composition (e.g. brass can be 30-40% zinc). These are properties of mixtures, not compounds.

items.question: Which statement about a saturated solution is CORRECT?

options.A: More solute can always be added
options.B: No more solute can dissolve at that temperature

items.explanation: Saturated solution holds maximum possible solute at a given temperature. On heating, solubility increases and more solute can dissolve.

items.question: Three formulas for concentration of a solution are mass/mass %, mass/volume %, and volume/volume %. For a gas dissolved in liquid, which formula is most appropriate?
items.explanation: For gas in liquid solutions (like CO2 in soda water), volume by volume percentage is most convenient since measuring gas mass is difficult. Mass by mass is easier for solid solutes.

items.question: In centrifugation of a colloidal solution, particles separate because:

options.A: particles settle due to gravity alone
options.B: centrifugal force many times greater than gravity forces colloidal particles

items.explanation: Colloidal particles are too small to settle under gravity (stable). Centrifugation applies centrifugal force far greater than gravity, forcing colloidal particles to the bottom.

items.question: Copper sulphate solution does NOT show Tyndall effect but starch solution shows it. Reason:

options.B: starch particles (1-1000 nm) scatter light; copper sulphate particles
options.C: starch solution is heterogeneous while copper sulphate is homogeneous

items.explanation: Tyndall effect needs particles of 1-1000 nm range. Starch forms a colloidal solution (1-1000 nm) and scatters light. Copper sulphate forms true solution (<1 nm) -- particles too small to scatter visible light.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
The CONCENTRATION of a solution is the amount (mass or volume) of solute present
in a given amount (mass or volume) of solution.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Depending on amount of solute, a solution can be dilute, concentrated, or
saturated.
DILUTE: Less solute in given amount of solvent.
CONCENTRATED: More solute in given amount of solvent.
SATURATED: No more solute can dissolve at that temperature.
SOLUBILITY: Amount of solute present in saturated solution at given temperature.
UNSATURATED: More solute can still be dissolved.
Solubility increases with temperature for most solid solutes.

sections.label: FORMULAS:
items: = (Mass of solute / Mass of solution) x 100
= (Mass of solute / Volume of solution) x 100
= (Volume of solute / Volume of solution) x 100
40 g common salt in 320 g water.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 2.3:
sections.aim:
To show that different substances have different solubilities and solubility
changes with temperature.
sections.materials:
Two beakers, 50 mL water each, salt, sugar or barium chloride, glass
rod, burner.
procedure: Add salt to one beaker and sugar/barium chloride to another with
continuous stirring. When no more dissolves, heat by 5 degrees C. Add more solute.
sections.observation:
Different amounts dissolve at same temperature. More dissolves on
heating.
sections.conclusion:
Different substances have different solubilities. Solubility increases
with temperature.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is the difference between a saturated and an unsaturated
items.answer:
SATURATED SOLUTION: A solution in which no more solute can be dissolved at a
given temperature. Solute amount = solubility at that temperature.
UNSATURATED SOLUTION: A solution in which more solute can still be dissolved at
a given temperature. Solute amount is less than solubility.
Example: If 36 g NaCl dissolves in 100 g water at 293 K (saturated), adding
less than 36 g gives unsaturated solution.

items.question: What are the three ways to express concentration of a solution?
items.answer:
Three ways to express concentration:

1. Mass by mass percentage:
= (Mass of solute / Mass of solution) x 100
Used when solute is a solid dissolved in liquid.

2. Mass by volume percentage:
= (Mass of solute / Volume of solution) x 100
Used commonly in medicine and pharmacy.

3. Volume by volume percentage:
= (Volume of solute / Volume of solution) x 100
Used when both solute and solvent are liquids, or for gas in liquid.

items.question: A solution contains 10 g of glucose dissolved in 90 g of water.
items.answer:
Given:
Mass of solute (glucose) = 10 g
Mass of solvent (water) = 90 g
Mass of solution = 10 + 90 = 100 g

Mass by mass % = (Mass of solute / Mass of solution) x 100
= (10 / 100) x 100
= 10%

Whether more glucose can dissolve:
At room temperature (about 293 K), solubility of glucose in water is about 91 g
per 100 g water. Since we have only 10 g in 90 g water (much less than maximum),
this is an UNSATURATED solution. More glucose can be dissolved.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: A saturated solution is one in which:

options.A: the solvent is completely used up
options.B: no more solute can dissolve at that temperature
options.C: the solution appears very dark in colour
options.D: solute and solvent are present in equal amounts

items.explanation: Saturated solution holds maximum possible solute at a given temperature. Colour depends on the solute, not saturation level.

items.question: Mass by mass percentage of a solution with 5 g salt in 95 g water:
items.explanation: Mass of solution = 5 + 95 = 100 g. Percentage = (5/100) x 100 = 5%.

items.question: On heating a saturated solution of salt, what happens?

options.C: More salt can now be dissolved

items.explanation: Solubility of most salts increases with temperature. At higher temperature, the saturated solution can dissolve more solute -- it becomes unsaturated at higher temperature.

items.question: Which formula gives concentration in mass by volume percentage?

options.A: (Mass of solute / Mass of solution) x 100
options.B: (Mass of solute / Volume of solution) x 100
options.C: (Volume of solute / Volume of solution) x 100
options.D: (Volume of solute / Mass of solution) x 100

items.explanation: Mass by volume % = (Mass of solute / Volume of solution) x 100. Option A is mass by mass %, Option C is volume by volume %.

items.question: 40 g of NaCl is dissolved in 360 g of water. Mass by mass percentage of NaCl is:
items.explanation: Mass of solution = 40 + 360 = 400 g. Mass % = (40/400) x 100 = 10%. Note: Option B (11.1%) is for 40 g in 320 g water (Example 2.1 from textbook).

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
A SUSPENSION is a heterogeneous mixture in which the solute particles do not
dissolve but remain suspended throughout the bulk of the medium. Particles of a
suspension are visible to the naked eye.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Suspension is a heterogeneous mixture.
Particles visible to naked eye (size >1000 nm).
Particles scatter a beam of light -- path visible.
Unstable -- solute particles settle down on standing.
Components can be separated by filtration.
When particles settle, suspension breaks and no longer scatters light.
Examples: Muddy water, chalk in water, wheat flour in water.

items.question: What is a suspension? Give two properties.
items.answer:
A SUSPENSION is a heterogeneous mixture in which the solute particles do not
dissolve but remain suspended throughout the medium. Particles are visible.
Properties:
1. Unstable -- particles settle on standing.
2. Can be separated by filtration.

items.question: How does a suspension differ from a solution? Give three points.
items.answer:
Suspension vs Solution:

1. Nature: Suspension is heterogeneous; solution is homogeneous.
2. Particle size: Suspension >1000 nm (visible); solution <1 nm (invisible).
3. Stability: Suspension unstable (settles); solution stable (does not settle).
Also: Suspension can be filtered; solution cannot be filtered.
Also: Suspension scatters light; solution does not scatter light.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Which of the following is a suspension?
items.explanation: Muddy water has large mud particles (>1000 nm) that are visible and settle on standing -- it is a suspension. Salt water and lemonade are solutions. Milk is a colloid.

items.question: Suspension particles can be separated by:
items.explanation: Suspension particles (>1000 nm) are too large to pass through ordinary filter paper. Filtration separates them as residue. Centrifugation is for colloids. Evaporation and distillation are for solutions.

items.question: A suspension is unstable because:

options.C: large particles (>1000 nm) settle under gravity when undisturbed

items.explanation: Suspension particles are large (>1000 nm) and heavy enough to settle under gravity when left undisturbed. Colloidal and solution particles are too small to settle.

items.question: When suspension particles settle down, the suspension:

options.C: breaks and no longer scatters light

items.explanation: Tyndall effect in suspension is due to suspended particles. When particles settle, no colloidal/suspended particles remain in medium -- light scattering stops and the suspension breaks.

items.question: Wheat flour in water is a suspension, not a solution. Proof is:

options.B: flour particles settle on standing and can be filtered from water

items.explanation: Flour forms a suspension -- particles are large (>1000 nm), visible, settle on standing (unstable), and can be separated by filtration (residue on filter paper). A solution would not settle or filter.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
A COLLOID or COLLOIDAL SOLUTION is a heterogeneous mixture in which the particles
are uniformly spread throughout the solution. Particles are too small to be seen
with naked eye but large enough to scatter a beam of light (Tyndall effect).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Colloid is heterogeneous (appears homogeneous due to small particle size).
Particle size: 1 nm to 1000 nm.
Particles not visible to naked eye.
Shows TYNDALL EFFECT -- scatters beam of visible light.
Stable -- does not settle on standing.
Cannot be separated by ordinary filtration.
Separated by CENTRIFUGATION.
COMPONENTS OF COLLOID:
DISPERSED PHASE: The solute-like component (dispersed particles).
DISPERSION MEDIUM: The component in which dispersed phase is suspended.
TABLE 2.1: COMMON EXAMPLES OF COLLOIDS:
Dispersed Phase | Dispersion Medium | Type      | Example
Liquid          | Gas               | Aerosol   | Fog, clouds, mist
Solid           | Gas               | Aerosol   | Smoke, automobile exhaust
Gas             | Liquid            | Foam      | Shaving cream
Liquid          | Liquid            | Emulsion  | Milk, face cream
Solid           | Liquid            | Sol       | Milk of magnesia, mud
Gas             | Solid             | Foam      | Foam rubber, sponge, pumice
Liquid          | Solid             | Gel       | Jelly, cheese, butter
Solid           | Solid             | Solid Sol | Coloured gemstone, milky glass
TYNDALL EFFECT EXAMPLES:
1. Sunlight passing through canopy of a dense forest (mist = colloid).
2. Fine beam of light entering a room through a small hole (dust in air).

items.question: What is a colloidal solution? State two properties.
items.answer:
A COLLOIDAL SOLUTION is a heterogeneous mixture in which particles (1-1000 nm)
are uniformly spread throughout but too small to be seen with naked eye.
Properties:
1. Shows Tyndall effect -- scatters beam of light.
2. Stable -- particles do not settle on standing.

items.question: Name the two components of a colloid. Using Table 2.1, identify
items.answer:
Two components:
1. DISPERSED PHASE: Solute-like component (dispersed particles).
2. DISPERSION MEDIUM: Component in which dispersed phase is suspended.

Milk:
- Dispersed phase: Liquid (fat droplets).
- Dispersion medium: Liquid (water).
- Type: Emulsion.

Butter:
- Dispersed phase: Liquid (fat).
- Dispersion medium: Solid (protein-water network).
- Type: Gel.

items.question: What is the Tyndall effect? With two examples from daily life,
items.answer:
TYNDALL EFFECT: Scattering of a beam of visible light by colloidal particles,
making the path of light visible.

Examples:
1. Sunlight through forest canopy: Mist (water droplets in air = aerosol colloid,
1-1000 nm) scatters sunlight -- beam visible through trees.
2. Light through room window: Dust and smoke particles in air (colloidal size)
scatter the light beam -- path visible in the room.

Why colloids show Tyndall effect but solutions do not:
- Colloidal particles: 1-1000 nm -- in the size range of visible light wavelength
(400-700 nm). They deflect the light beam, making it visible.
- Solution particles: less than 1 nm -- far smaller than visible light wavelength.
They cannot deflect light -- beam passes through invisible.
- This is why copper sulphate solution does not show Tyndall effect, but starch
solution (colloidal) does.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Which type of colloid is shaving cream?
items.explanation: Shaving cream = gas (air bubbles) dispersed in liquid = Foam type colloid. Emulsion is liquid in liquid, Sol is solid in liquid, Aerosol is liquid in gas.

items.question: Colloidal particles are separated by:
items.explanation: Colloidal particles (1-1000 nm) pass through ordinary filter paper pores so filtration fails. Centrifugation applies strong force to separate them.

items.question: Starch solution shows Tyndall effect because:

options.B: starch particles (1-1000 nm range) scatter visible light

items.explanation: Tyndall effect requires particle size 1-1000 nm. Starch forms colloidal solution in this range, so particles scatter visible light. Colour and concentration do not determine Tyndall effect.

items.question: In the colloid "mud", the dispersed phase and dispersion medium are:
items.explanation: Mud = solid particles (clay, sand) dispersed in liquid (water) = Sol type colloid (solid in liquid). From Table 2.1, Sol examples include mud and milk of magnesia.

items.question: Smoke from a fire shows Tyndall effect but pure air does not. This is because:

options.B: smoke contains solid carbon particles of colloidal size that scatter light;

items.explanation: Smoke = solid (carbon) in gas (air) = Aerosol colloid. Carbon particles (1-1000 nm) scatter light (Tyndall effect). Pure air molecules (<1 nm) are too small to scatter visible light -- no Tyndall effect.

items.question: Coloured gemstone is an example of which type of colloid, and what are its dispersed phase and dispersion medium?

options.C: Solid Sol -- solid dispersed in solid

items.explanation: Coloured gemstone = coloured mineral (solid, dispersed phase) embedded in rock (solid, dispersion medium) = Solid Sol. From Table 2.1: Solid dispersed in Solid gives Solid Sol examples: coloured gemstone, milky glass.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
A PHYSICAL CHANGE is a change in which no new substance is formed. Physical
properties change but chemical nature remains the same. It is generally reversible.

A CHEMICAL CHANGE is a change in which a new substance with completely different
properties is formed. Chemical nature changes. It is also called a CHEMICAL
REACTION. Generally irreversible.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: PHYSICAL CHANGES:
Only physical properties (colour, shape, size, state) change.
No new substance formed.
Generally reversible.
Chemical composition unchanged.
Examples: Melting of ice, boiling of water, dissolving salt in water, cutting
of trees, making a fruit salad with raw fruits, melting of butter.
CHEMICAL CHANGES:
New substances with new chemical properties formed.
Change in composition occurs.
Generally irreversible.
Examples: Rusting of iron (Fe + O2 + H2O -> Fe2O3.nH2O), burning of paper and
wood, cooking of food, digestion of food, passing electric current through water
(H2O -> H2 + O2), growth of a plant.
HOW TO IDENTIFY:
New substance with new properties formed? -> Chemical change.
Properties change but composition same? -> Physical change.
BOTH IN ONE EVENT:
Burning of a candle:
Melting of wax = PHYSICAL (solid to liquid, reversible, no new substance).
Burning of wax vapour = CHEMICAL (new substances CO2 + H2O formed, irreversible).

items.question: Define physical change and chemical change. Give one example each.
items.answer:
PHYSICAL CHANGE: Change in which no new substance is formed. Physical properties
change but chemical nature stays same. Generally reversible.
Example: Melting of ice to water.

CHEMICAL CHANGE: Change in which a new substance with different chemical
properties is formed. Generally irreversible.
Example: Rusting of iron (new substance -- iron oxide formed).

items.question: Why is interconversion of states of matter a physical change?
items.answer:
Interconversion of states (ice -> water -> steam) is a physical change because:
1. No new substance formed -- all three are H2O (water).
2. Chemical nature of water does not change in any state.
3. Reversible -- steam condenses to water, water freezes to ice.

items.question: Classify the following with reasons: (a) rusting of almirah
items.answer:
(a) Rusting of almirah: CHEMICAL CHANGE.
Reason: Iron reacts with oxygen and moisture to form iron oxide (rust) -- a new
substance with different properties (reddish, brittle). Irreversible.

(b) Dissolving common salt in water: PHYSICAL CHANGE.
Reason: Salt (NaCl) retains chemical nature. No new substance formed. Salt can
be recovered by evaporation. Reversible.

(c) Burning of paper: CHEMICAL CHANGE.
Reason: Paper (cellulose) reacts with oxygen to form CO2, water vapour, and ash.
New substances with completely different properties formed. Irreversible.

items.question: Give two examples each of physical and chemical changes from daily
items.answer:
PHYSICAL CHANGES:

1. Melting of butter in a pan:
- Solid butter becomes liquid.
- No new substance formed; fat composition unchanged.
- Reversible (solidifies on cooling).

2. Boiling of water to form steam:
- State changes (liquid to gas).
- Same chemical formula H2O; no new substance.
- Reversible (steam condenses back to water).

CHEMICAL CHANGES:

1. Cooking of food:
- Raw food undergoes reactions on heating.
- New substances with new taste, smell, texture formed.
- Irreversible (cooked food cannot become raw again).

2. Passing electric current through water:
- Water (H2O) splits into hydrogen gas and oxygen gas.
- New substances with completely different properties formed.
- Irreversible.

items.question: "Burning a candle involves both physical and chemical changes."
items.answer:
Burning a candle involves BOTH types:

PHYSICAL CHANGE:
- Wax near flame melts due to heat (solid to liquid).
- Liquid wax rises through wick and vaporises (liquid to gas).
- No new substance formed in melting and vaporisation.
- Melted wax can solidify again -- reversible.

CHEMICAL CHANGE:
- Wax vapour burns in presence of oxygen.
- New substances formed -- carbon dioxide (CO2) and water vapour (H2O).
- Products have completely different properties from wax.
- Burning is irreversible.

Conclusion: Melting of wax = physical change; combustion of wax vapour = chemical
change. Both occur simultaneously in a burning candle.

items.question: What is the difference between physical and chemical changes?
items.answer:
PHYSICAL CHANGE: No new substance formed, physical properties change, reversible,
chemical composition unchanged.
CHEMICAL CHANGE: New substance with different properties formed, generally
irreversible, chemical composition changes.

PHYSICAL CHANGES:

1. Melting of butter in a pan:
No new substance; butter composition (fat) unchanged; reversible (solidifies).

2. Boiling of water to form steam:
State changes (liquid to gas); same H2O; reversible (condensation).

3. Dissolving common salt in water:
Salt retains chemical nature (NaCl); recoverable by evaporation; reversible.

4. Making a fruit salad with raw fruits:
Only physical mixing; no new substance; fruits retain chemical properties.

5. Cutting of trees:
Only shape and size change; chemical nature of wood (cellulose) unchanged.

CHEMICAL CHANGES:

1. Rusting of almirah:
Fe + O2 + H2O -> Fe2O3.nH2O (rust); new substance; irreversible.

2. Passing electric current through water:
H2O -> H2 + O2 (electrolysis); new gases with different properties; irreversible.

3. Burning of paper and wood:
Paper/wood + O2 -> CO2 + H2O + ash; new substances; irreversible.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Which of the following is a physical change?
items.explanation: Melting of ice is physical -- state changes (solid to liquid), same H2O, no new substance, reversible. Burning, rusting, and cooking are chemical changes.

items.question: Which is an example of a chemical change?
items.explanation: Digestion uses enzymes to break food into glucose, amino acids, etc. -- new substances with different properties. Options A, B, D are physical changes.

items.question: Passing electric current through water is a chemical change because:

options.C: new substances hydrogen and oxygen gases are formed

items.explanation: Electrolysis produces H2 and O2 -- completely new substances with different properties from water. Formation of new substance = chemical change.

items.question: Why is dissolving common salt in water a physical change?

options.A: A new substance NaCl is formed
options.C: Salt retains its chemical nature and can be recovered by evaporation

items.explanation: Salt (NaCl) retains chemical identity and is recovered by evaporation -- no chemical reaction occurred. Colour does not determine type of change.

items.question: Growth of a plant involves:
items.explanation: Growth involves chemical changes (photosynthesis, respiration forming new substances) and physical changes (increase in size and shape). Both occur during plant growth.

items.question: Burning of a candle is an example of:
items.explanation: Melting of wax is physical (solid to liquid, reversible, same substance). Burning of wax vapour is chemical (CO2 and H2O formed, irreversible, new substances). Both occur simultaneously.

topics.topic_name: WHAT ARE THE TYPES OF PURE SUBSTANCES?

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
Pure substances are classified into ELEMENTS and COMPOUNDS on the basis of their
chemical composition.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: An element cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical reactions.
A compound is composed of two or more elements chemically combined in fixed
proportion.
Properties of a compound are completely different from its constituent elements.
Properties of a mixture are the same as those of its constituting elements or
compounds.
Compounds can be broken down into elements only by chemical or electrochemical
reactions.

items.question: What is a compound? Give two examples.
items.answer:
A COMPOUND is a substance composed of two or more different types of elements,
chemically combined in a fixed proportion. Its properties are completely different
from constituent elements.
Examples:
1. Water (H2O) -- hydrogen and oxygen in fixed ratio 1:8 by mass.
2. Common salt (NaCl) -- sodium and chlorine in fixed ratio.

items.question: Who first used the term "element" and who first defined it
items.answer:
Robert Boyle was the first scientist to use the term "element" in 1661.
Antoine Laurent Lavoisier (1743-94), a French chemist, was the first to establish
an experimentally useful definition of an element as a basic form of matter that
cannot be broken down into simpler substances by chemical reactions.

items.question: Give three differences between metals and non-metals with examples.
items.answer:
1. Conductivity:
Metals: Good conductors of heat and electricity. Example: copper, iron.
Non-metals: Poor conductors of heat and electricity. Example: sulphur.

2. Physical appearance:
Metals: Lustrous (shiny), silvery-grey or golden-yellow. Example: gold, silver.
Non-metals: Variety of colours, not lustrous. Example: yellow sulphur, red
phosphorus.

3. Malleability and ductility:
Metals: Malleable (beaten into sheets) and ductile (drawn into wires).
Example: gold, copper.
Non-metals: Not malleable or ductile -- brittle if solid. Example: sulphur
crumbles when hammered.

items.question: From Activity 2.4, explain how the product of Group II (heated
items.answer:
Evidence that Group II product (iron sulphide, FeS) is a compound:

1. Magnetic property: Iron filings in Group I mixture are attracted to magnet.
Iron sulphide (FeS) in Group II is NOT attracted to magnet -- property changed.

2. Colour: Mix of grey iron + yellow sulphur. FeS is black coloured -- different
from both elements.

3. Reaction with acid: Group I (mixture) + dilute acid gives hydrogen gas (H2)
-- colourless, no smell. Group II (FeS) + dilute acid gives hydrogen sulphide
(H2S) -- colourless, rotten egg smell. Completely different gas = new substance.

4. Fixed composition: FeS always has iron and sulphur in fixed ratio (7:4 by
mass) -- cannot vary like a mixture.

All these prove FeS is a compound, not a mixture.

items.question: What are the properties of a compound? How do they differ from a
items.answer:
Properties of a Compound:
1. Fixed composition -- elements combined in fixed proportion by mass.
2. Completely different properties from constituent elements.
3. Cannot be separated by physical methods.
4. Formed by chemical reaction between elements.

Differences from Mixture:

Point         | Compound                      | Mixture
--------------|-------------------------------|--------------------------------
Composition   | Fixed (always same ratio)     | Variable (any proportion)
Properties    | New, different properties     | Retains properties of components
Separation    | Chemical/electrochemical only | Physical methods (magnet, filter)
Formation     | Chemical reaction needed      | Physical mixing (no reaction)

items.question: "Properties of a compound are completely different from its
items.answer:
JUSTIFICATION WITH IRON AND SULPHUR (Activity 2.4):

Iron (Fe): Grey metal, magnetic, reacts with dilute H2SO4 to give H2 gas.
Sulphur (S): Yellow non-metal, non-magnetic, does not react easily with dilute
acid.

Heating them forms Iron Sulphide (FeS):
Fe + S -> FeS (at high temperature)

Properties of Iron Sulphide (FeS):
- Colour: BLACK -- different from grey iron and yellow sulphur.
- Magnetic: NOT magnetic -- iron was magnetic; property completely changed.
- Reaction with acid: Gives H2S gas (rotten egg smell) -- different from H2.

FeS has COMPLETELY DIFFERENT properties from both iron and sulphur. This proves
the statement.

TABLE 2.2 -- MIXTURES vs COMPOUNDS:

Mixtures                                | Compounds
----------------------------------------|--------------------------------------
Elements/compounds mix with no new      | Elements react to form new compounds.
compound formed.                        |
Variable composition.                   | Fixed composition always.
Shows properties of constituent         | Totally different properties.
substances.                             |
Separated fairly easily by physical     | Separated only by chemical or
methods.                                | electrochemical reactions.

Example: Iron + Sulphur (mixed) = mixture (magnetic, H2 with acid).
Iron + Sulphur (heated) = FeS compound (non-magnetic, H2S with acid).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Which of the following is an element?
items.explanation: Iron (Fe) is an element -- cannot be broken into simpler substances. Water (H2O) and salt (NaCl) are compounds. Air is a mixture.

items.question: Which is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature?
items.explanation: Mercury is the only METAL liquid at room temperature. Bromine is a non-metal that is liquid. Gallium and cesium become liquid slightly above room temperature (303 K).

items.question: A compound differs from a mixture because a compound:

options.C: has fixed composition and completely new properties
options.D: can be separated by physical methods

items.explanation: Compound has fixed composition and completely different properties from constituent elements. Options A, B, D are characteristics of mixtures.

items.question: In Activity 2.4, Group I (iron + sulphur mixed) gave H2 gas with acid but Group II (heated iron sulphide) gave H2S gas. This proves:

options.B: compound has completely different chemical properties from the mixture
options.C: sulphur and iron are the same element

items.explanation: Different gases (H2 vs H2S) prove that iron sulphide (FeS) compound has completely different chemical properties from the iron + sulphur mixture.

items.question: Which pair is correctly classified?
items.explanation: Sodium (Na) = element (cannot break further). Water (H2O) = compound (H and O in fixed proportion). Air = mixture, Soil = mixture, Gold = element, Oxygen = element.

items.question: How many elements are naturally occurring?
items.explanation: 92 elements are naturally occurring. The rest (total >100) are man-made synthetic elements. 11 elements are gaseous at room temperature.

items.question: Iron sulphide (FeS) is not attracted to magnet, but iron filings are attracted. This is because:

options.B: chemical change formed FeS compound with completely different properties from
options.C: the mixture lost magnetic property on mixing
options.D: a physical change occurred that is reversible

items.explanation: Heating iron and sulphur causes chemical change forming FeS. Compound has completely new properties -- loss of magnetic property proves new substance formed (not just a mixture of iron and sulphur).

items.question: "The composition of water is always H2O (1:8 H:O by mass) wherever found." This illustrates:

options.A: compounds have fixed composition (law of definite proportions)
options.B: all compounds have the same number of elements
options.D: water and alcohol are the same compound

items.explanation: Law of definite proportions -- a compound always has the same elements in the same mass ratio regardless of source. Water (H2O) always has H:O = 1:8 by mass. This is a key property of compounds distinguishing them from mixtures (variable composition).

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
An ELEMENT is a basic form of matter that cannot be broken down into simpler
substances by chemical reactions. (Lavoisier, 1743-94)

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: HISTORY:
Robert Boyle: First used term "element" (1661).
Antoine Laurent Lavoisier (1743-94): First experimental definition of element.

sections.label: CLASSIFICATION:
sections.text:
Elements classified as METALS, NON-METALS, and METALLOIDS.

METALS -- Properties:
1. Have lustre (shine).
2. Silvery-grey or golden-yellow colour.
3. Conduct heat and electricity.
4. Ductile -- can be drawn into wires.
5. Malleable -- can be hammered into thin sheets.
6. Sonorous -- make ringing sound when hit.
Examples: gold, silver, copper, iron, sodium, potassium.
Special: Mercury is the only metal liquid at room temperature.

NON-METALS -- Properties:
1. Display variety of colours.
2. Poor conductors of heat and electricity.
3. Not lustrous, sonorous, or malleable.
Examples: hydrogen, oxygen, iodine, carbon (coal, coke), bromine, chlorine.

METALLOIDS:
- Intermediate properties between metals and non-metals.
Examples: boron, silicon, germanium.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS:
sections.text:
- Total known elements: more than 100.
- Naturally occurring: 92. Man-made: rest.
- Majority of elements are solid.
- 11 elements are gaseous at room temperature.
- 2 elements are liquid at room temperature: mercury (metal) and bromine
(non-metal).
- Gallium and cesium become liquid slightly above room temperature (303 K).

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Name any four properties of metals.
items.answer:
Properties of metals:
1. Have lustre (shine) -- e.g. gold shines.
2. Good conductors of heat and electricity -- e.g. copper wire conducts.
3. Malleable -- can be beaten into thin sheets -- e.g. aluminium foil.
4. Ductile -- can be drawn into wires -- e.g. copper drawn into electric wire.

items.question: How are non-metals different from metals? Give three points with
items.answer:
1. Conductivity:
Metals: Good conductors of heat and electricity (copper, iron).
Non-metals: Poor conductors (sulphur, carbon except graphite).

2. Lustre:
Metals: Lustrous/shiny (gold, silver).
Non-metals: Not lustrous (sulphur is dull yellow; iodine has slight lustre).

3. Malleability and Ductility:
Metals: Malleable and ductile (gold can be drawn into thin wire).
Non-metals: Brittle -- break when hammered (sulphur crumbles, carbon breaks).

items.question: Give additional facts about elements: How many are naturally
items.answer:
1. Number of naturally occurring elements: 92.
Total elements known: more than 100. The rest are man-made synthetic elements.

2. Elements in gaseous state at room temperature: 11.
Examples: hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, chlorine, fluorine, neon, argon, helium,
krypton, xenon, radon.

3. Two elements liquid at room temperature:
- Mercury (Hg) -- only liquid metal.
- Bromine (Br) -- only liquid non-metal.
Note: Gallium and cesium become liquid slightly above room temperature (303 K).

4. Two metalloids (intermediate properties):
- Silicon (Si) -- used in semiconductors.
- Germanium (Ge) -- used in electronics.

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Which property is NOT shown by metals?
items.explanation: Metals are GOOD conductors of electricity -- this is a key property. Poor conductivity is a property of non-metals. Lustre, malleability, and sonorousness are metal properties.

items.question: Which two elements are liquid at room temperature?
items.explanation: Mercury (metal) and bromine (non-metal) are the only two elements liquid at room temperature. Gallium and cesium become liquid slightly above room temperature (303 K), not at room temperature.

items.question: Elements with intermediate properties between metals and non-metals are called:
items.explanation: Metalloids (boron, silicon, germanium) have intermediate properties between metals and non-metals. Alloys are mixtures of metals. Compounds are chemically combined substances.

items.question: Which of the following correctly states the number of naturally occurring elements?
items.explanation: 92 elements occur naturally. Total elements known are more than 100. The rest beyond 92 are man-made (synthetic) elements created in laboratory.

items.question: Carbon is a non-metal. Which property of non-metals does it show?

options.C: Generally a poor conductor (though graphite form conducts)

items.explanation: Carbon as coal/coke is a non-metal -- poor conductor. However, graphite (a form of carbon) is an exception that conducts electricity. Most non-metals are poor conductors of heat and electricity.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
A COMPOUND is a substance composed of two or more different types of elements,
chemically combined together in a fixed proportion. Properties are completely
different from constituent elements.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Elements in compound combined in fixed proportion by mass.
Properties completely different from constituent elements.
Cannot be separated by physical methods.
Separated only by chemical or electrochemical reactions.
Composition always fixed (e.g. water always H2O, H:O = 1:8 by mass).
Formed by chemical reaction (energy change usually occurs).

sections.label: ACTIVITY 2.4:
sections.aim: To distinguish between a mixture and a compound using iron and sulphur.
sections.materials:
5 g iron filings, 3 g sulphur powder, china dish, magnet, carbon
disulphide, dilute sulphuric acid/hydrochloric acid.
procedure: GROUP I: Mix and crush iron filings + sulphur powder (do NOT heat).
GROUP II: Mix iron filings + sulphur; heat strongly till red hot; let cool.
Both groups: Check magnetism, dissolve in carbon disulphide, add dilute acid.
sections.observation:
GROUP I (Mixture Fe + S):
- Both iron and sulphur visible separately.
- Magnetic -- iron attracted to magnet; sulphur not.
- Iron dissolves in carbon disulphide; sulphur also dissolves.
- Dilute acid: Hydrogen gas (H2) -- colourless, odourless, combustible.

GROUP II (Compound FeS):
- Uniform black appearance; neither iron nor sulphur identifiable.
- NOT magnetic -- not attracted to magnet.
- Does not dissolve in carbon disulphide.
- Dilute acid: Hydrogen sulphide gas (H2S) -- colourless, rotten egg smell.
sections.conclusion:
Group I = mixture (retains properties of iron and sulphur).
Group II = compound FeS (completely new properties; Fe:S in fixed ratio 7:4).
Compound has completely different properties from its constituent elements.

TABLE 2.2: DIFFERENCES BETWEEN MIXTURES AND COMPOUNDS:

Mixtures                              | Compounds
--------------------------------------|--------------------------------------
Elements/compounds mix; no new        | Elements react to form new compounds.
compound formed.                      |
Variable composition.                 | Fixed composition always.
Shows properties of constituents.     | Totally different new properties.
Separated by physical methods         | Separated only by chemical or
(fairly easily).                      | electrochemical reactions.

GRAPHICAL ORGANISER:

MATTER (Solid, Liquid, Gas)
|
+-- PURE SUBSTANCE
|     |
|     +-- ELEMENTS (Cannot be broken into simpler substances)
|     |   Examples: copper, oxygen, iron, hydrogen, mercury
|     |
|     +-- COMPOUNDS (Fixed composition; broken by chemical means only)
|         Examples: water, methane, sugar, salt, calcium carbonate
|
+-- MIXTURES (No fixed composition)
|
+-- HOMOGENEOUS (Uniform composition)
|   Examples: sugar in water, salt in water, air
|
+-- HETEROGENEOUS (Non-uniform composition)
Examples: sand and salt, water in oil, soil

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: What is a compound? What is the key difference from an element?
items.answer:
A COMPOUND is a substance composed of two or more different types of elements,
chemically combined in a fixed proportion, with completely new properties.
Key difference from element:
- Element has only one type of atom; cannot be broken down further by chemical
reactions.
- Compound has two or more different types of atoms combined; can be broken into
elements by chemical or electrochemical reactions.

items.question: From Activity 2.4, give three pieces of evidence that iron sulphide
items.answer:
1. Magnetic property changed: Fe + S mixture attracted to magnet (iron is
magnetic). FeS compound NOT attracted -- completely new property.

2. Colour changed: Grey iron + yellow sulphur mix shows both colours. FeS is
uniformly black -- new substance.

3. Gas with acid changed: Mixture + acid gives H2 (no smell). FeS + acid gives
H2S (rotten egg smell) -- completely different new substance formed.

items.question: Classify the following into elements, compounds, and mixtures:
items.answer:
ELEMENTS (cannot be broken further by chemical reactions):
- Sodium (Na)
- Silver (Ag)
- Tin (Sn)
- Silicon (Si)
- Coal (C -- carbon element)

COMPOUNDS (two or more elements in fixed proportion):
- Calcium carbonate (CaCO3 -- calcium + carbon + oxygen)
- Soap (sodium/potassium salts of fatty acids)
- Methane (CH4 -- carbon + hydrogen)
- Carbon dioxide (CO2 -- carbon + oxygen)

MIXTURES (variable composition):
- Soil (sand + clay + minerals + organic matter)
- Sugar solution (sugar + water)
- Air (N2 + O2 + CO2 + Ar, etc.)
- Blood (RBC + WBC + plasma + proteins)

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

items.question: Which of the following is a compound?
items.explanation: Water (H2O) is a compound -- two elements (hydrogen and oxygen) combined in fixed ratio 1:8 by mass. Iron, sodium, and silicon are elements -- single type of atom.

items.question: Iron sulphide (FeS) is NOT attracted to a magnet but iron filings are. This shows:

options.A: iron lost its property on mixing
options.B: FeS is a compound with completely different properties from iron

items.explanation: Chemical reaction between iron and sulphur forms FeS compound with completely new properties. Loss of magnetic property is direct evidence that a new substance (not a mixture) has formed.

items.question: Which method can break a compound into its constituent elements?
items.explanation: Compounds can only be broken by chemical or electrochemical reactions. Example: Electrolysis breaks water (H2O) into hydrogen and oxygen. Filtration, distillation, and decantation are physical methods -- they cannot break compounds.

items.question: "Water is always H2O wherever it is found." This illustrates:

options.B: compounds have fixed composition (law of definite proportions)

items.explanation: Compounds always have the same elements in the same fixed mass ratio regardless of source -- law of definite proportions. Water always has H:O = 1:8 by mass. This differentiates compounds from mixtures (variable composition).

items.question: From Activity 2.4, Group I (mixture) gave H2 gas with dilute acid, but Group II (FeS compound) gave H2S gas. This is proof that:

options.B: iron and sulphur reacted physically in Group II
options.C: FeS has completely different chemical properties from Fe and S -- it is a
options.D: dilute acid reacts differently with same substance

items.explanation: Different gases produced (H2 from Fe, H2S from FeS) prove FeS has completely different chemical properties from its constituent elements. This is a defining property of compounds -- new properties, not those of constituents.

items.question: Which of the following pairs correctly represents a compound and its constituent elements?
items.explanation: Water (H2O) is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen in fixed ratio 1:8 by mass. Air is a mixture (variable N2/O2 ratio). Brass is an alloy/mixture (not compound). Soil is a heterogeneous mixture.

sections.label: EXERCISE 2.1:
sections.raw:
Steps for making tea using the words solution, solvent, solute, dissolve,
soluble, insoluble, filtrate, residue:
Take water (solvent) in a pan. Add tea leaves -- they are insoluble in water.
Pour the tea through filter paper in a funnel. The tea liquor (filtrate) passes
through. Tea leaves remain as residue. Add sugar (solute) to the filtrate and
stir. Sugar dissolves (is soluble in water) to form a solution. Add milk. Heat
and the tea is ready.

sections.label: EXERCISE 2.3:
sections.raw:
(a) Saturated solution: A solution in which no more solute can be dissolved at
a given temperature. The amount present is its solubility.
(b) Pure substance: A substance consisting of a single type of particle. All
constituent particles are chemically the same. Has characteristic fixed properties.
(c) Colloid: A heterogeneous mixture in which particle size is 1-1000 nm. Appears
homogeneous, stable, shows Tyndall effect.
(d) Suspension: A heterogeneous mixture in which solute particles do not dissolve,
remain suspended, are visible to naked eye, and settle on standing.

sections.label: EXERCISE 2.4: Classify as homogeneous or heterogeneous:
sections.raw:
- Soda water: HOMOGENEOUS (CO2 gas uniformly dissolved in water)
- Wood: HETEROGENEOUS (different cells and fibres, non-uniform)
- Air: HOMOGENEOUS (uniform mixture of gases)
- Soil: HETEROGENEOUS (sand, clay, minerals unevenly distributed)
- Vinegar: HOMOGENEOUS (acetic acid uniformly dissolved in water)
- Filtered tea: HOMOGENEOUS (uniform solution after removing tea leaves)

sections.label: EXERCISE 2.5: How to confirm a colourless liquid is pure water:
sections.raw:
- Check boiling point: pure water boils at exactly 100 degrees C (373 K) at 1 atm.
- Check freezing point: pure water freezes at exactly 0 degrees C (273 K).
- Evaporation test: pure water leaves no residue on complete evaporation.
Any deviation suggests impurities (mixture).

sections.label: EXERCISE 2.6: Pure substances:
sections.raw:
(a) Ice: Pure substance (H2O -- compound)
(b) Milk: NOT pure (colloidal mixture of fat, protein, water)
(c) Iron: Pure substance (Fe -- element)
(d) Hydrochloric acid: Pure substance (HCl -- compound)
(e) Calcium oxide: Pure substance (CaO -- compound)
(f) Mercury: Pure substance (Hg -- element)
(g) Brick: NOT pure (mixture of clay, sand, minerals)
(h) Wood: NOT pure (mixture of cellulose, lignin, water, minerals)
(i) Air: NOT pure (mixture of N2, O2, CO2, Ar, etc.)

sections.label: EXERCISE 2.7: Solutions among mixtures:
sections.raw:
(a) Soil: NOT a solution (heterogeneous)
(b) Sea water: SOLUTION (homogeneous)
(c) Air: SOLUTION (homogeneous mixture of gases)
(d) Coal: NOT a solution (mixture of carbon compounds)
(e) Soda water: SOLUTION (CO2 uniformly dissolved in water)

sections.label: EXERCISE 2.8: Tyndall effect:
sections.raw:
(a) Salt solution: NO (true solution, particles <1 nm)
(b) Milk: YES (colloidal solution, particles 1-1000 nm)
(c) Copper sulphate solution: NO (true solution)
(d) Starch solution: YES (colloidal solution)

sections.label: EXERCISE 2.10: Chemical changes:
sections.raw:
(a) Growth of a plant: CHEMICAL (photosynthesis, respiration -- new substances)
(b) Rusting of iron: CHEMICAL (Fe2O3.nH2O -- new substance)
(c) Mixing of iron filings and sand: PHYSICAL (no new substance, separable)
(d) Cooking of food: CHEMICAL (new substances by heat)
(e) Digestion of food: CHEMICAL (enzymes break food into new substances)
(f) Freezing of water: PHYSICAL (state change, same H2O)
(g) Burning of candle: BOTH (melting = physical; combustion = chemical)
